; Core Email Authentication DNS Records
v=spf1 ip4:198.51.100.0/24 include:_spf.google.com -all
v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIGfMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBAQUAA4GNADCBiQKBgQD...
v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@company.com; pct=100;

content.tldr: Email authentication relies on the cryptographic triad of SPF, DKIM, and DMARC to prevent spoofing, detect message tampering, and enforce domain governance.
content.simple_explanation: The legacy Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) lacks built-in sender verification, allowing any client to send messages claiming any arbitrary 'From' address. Modern defense combines three standards: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) publishes a DNS list of authorized sending IP addresses. DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) applies a cryptographic signature to message headers verified via public keys published in DNS. Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) instructs recipient servers how to handle messages that fail SPF or DKIM (reject or quarantine).
content.real_world_example: A corporate wax seal and courier registry: SPF verifies the courier company is contracted by the firm; DKIM checks the unbroken embossed wax seal; DMARC instructs the recipient to shred the envelope if the courier or seal is invalid.
content.why_it_matters_and_pitfalls: Configuring DMARC in passive monitoring mode (`p=none`) generates telemetry reports but does not block spoofed phishing emails. Organizations must achieve strict enforcement (`p=reject`) to eliminate domain spoofing attacks.
